title: Influence of Cultural Practices on the Development of Brown Leaf Spot Disease in Rice
authors: Sintoo Prajapati, Ashutosh Kumar, Prem Chand Singh
affiliations: 1 Department of Plant Pathology, Rajaram Mahavidyalaya, Belaunakala, Barsathi, Jaunpur.
2 Department of Plant Pathology, M M P G College, Kalakankar, Pratapgarh.

blocks.x: Abstract:

Bipolaris oryzae, a fungus that causes brown leaf spot (BLS) of rice, is a universal disease that is threatening to the rice production. The previous historical record is rather notorious as it has been involved in disastrous losses in yields like the Bengal famine in 1943. Over the past few years, BLS has resurfaced as a major limitation in most of the rice-producing regions across the world. This paper will look at the effect of cultural farming practices on the development and severity of BLS. Field experiments were undertaken to determine how important agronomic factors - preparation of seedbed, planting technique, fertilizer regime, organic amendments, and sanitation of the crop - affect BLS incidence and rice yield. The findings showed that some of the conventional practices (e.g., dense planting and unbalanced nutrient application) contribute to increased severity of the disease, and superior practices (e.g., the use of clean seed, balanced nutrient applications, and sanitation of fields) have a significant negative effect on the development of BLS. As an example, an integrated cultural management that included the incorporation of improved nitrogen fertilizer split-application, incorporation of farmyard manure, line sowing and weed control reduced leaf spot severity by more than 50 percent and increased the grain production enormously compared with traditional approaches. These observations highlight the fact that cultural practices are very critical in regulating the severity of diseases. The discussion emphasizes the physiological and epidemiological causes of such outcomes, well-nourished and spaced rice crops are less susceptible to BLS and puts the findings in the perspective of sustainable disease management. Finally, the advocacy of good cultural practices across the world would reduce the brown leaf spot disease to protect the rice produce and the livelihoods of farmers. The study suggests that an integrated strategy involving the use of resistant varieties and better cultural methods would result in lasting control of BLS in the different rice agro-ecosystems.
Introduction:

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is the staple food of more than a half of the world population, but it is constantly undermined by the diseases which lower the production and quality of grains. One such internationally significant fungal disease of rice is brown leaf spot (BLS), which is caused by Bipolaris oryzae (teleomorph Cochliobolus miyabeanus). Initially reported in the 19th century, BLS is currently present in practically all rice-producing areas - wet tropical Asia as well as temperate ones - where rice is grown (Bhutia et al., 2025). The disease causes brown necrotic lesions on leaves and grains causing early leaf senescence, grain discoloration, and loss of yields. In most cases, BLS leads to a small decline in yields (approximately 4-10 percent) though in favorable conditions the effect can be devastating[1][2]. The devastating power of epidemics is demonstrated by historic outbreaks: in 1942, an epidemic of BLS wiped out rice fields in Bengal, India, which led to the Great Bengal Famine of 1943 in which millions of people died (Padmanabhan, 1973). During that epidemic, the loss of grain yield was up to 50-90 in the affected regions (Ghose et al., 1960; Padmanabhan, 1973). BLS is one of the most enduring and destructive rice diseases even in the contemporary times. The survey has shown that the disease has been prevalent in Asia, Africa, and the Americas, and the

INFLUENCE OF CULTURAL PRACTICES ON THE DEVELOPMENT OF BROWN LEAF SPOT DISEASE IN RICE. yield decrease has been up to 1 percent in farmers fields as per locale and management circumstances [1]. This diversity of the BLS severity is highly intertwined with environmental and cultural activities - i.e. the farming techniques and crop management approaches applied by the growers (Barnwal et al., 2013). BLS is a disease traditionally associated with poverty and poor farming techniques (and it is often known as a disease of the poor and of poor cultivation) (Barnwal et al., 2013), and it usually occurs in rice cultures that are not subjected to the best conditions of growth and development e.g., a lack of nutrients, water stress, or without proper field hygiene. As an example, rice cultivated in rainfed upland or using few inputs tend to be more affected by BLS than crops that are well controlled and irrigated[3][4]. Such observations are indicative that a change in cultural practices can help a significant amount in making rice less vulnerable to BLS. Such cultural factors as the seed health, sowing density, fertilization, irrigation, and crop rotation have been found to affect the vulnerability of the rice plant and the spread of the pathogen (Sunder et al., 2014). Nevertheless, the overall picture of the impacts of each practice on the development of the BLS should be provided to shape combined disease management plans. The paper discusses how significant cultural practices affect the occurrence of brown leaf spot disease in rice with the global view. We check the literature on the epidemiology of BLS in the context of the agronomic practices, outline field trials that evaluated particular management interventions, and state how those practices changed the result of diseases. Our hypothesis is, a sequence of enhanced cultural practices, such as the use of clean seed, equal fertilization, appropriate plant spacing, timely weeding and management of residues, will result in reduced severity of BLS and yields than that under traditional or suboptimal practices. Through the quantification of these effects, we will offer evidence based recommendation which can be implemented in any part of the world to decrease the attack of brown leaf spot by using sustainable and non chemical approaches. Finally, BLS management might be built on the improvement of cultural practices that may lead to better food security and higher income of farmers in rice-reliant areas.
Literature Review:

Brown leaf spot- It is a disease that is highly influenced by the environment and culture. Traditionally, BLS has been a common problem with rice crops that have been subjected to stress or neglect, and not in good health (Barnwal et al., 2013). The major literature has referred to a number of cultural and agronomic aspects that affect the development of the disease:

Seed health and variety: The BLS pathogen is seed-borne; infected seeds are the main inoculum, which causes early infection of seedlings, and causes the disease to be carried over between seasons (Kabore et al., 2025). Infection rates of rice seeds may be as low as below 1 percent and as high as 75 percent [1]. Cultural practices such as the use of disease-free or treated seed are thus important. Treatment of seeds - using fungicides or meeting with bio-control agents - can significantly reduce primary infection. As an illustration, the incidence of brown spots in rice seed was reduced by approximately 70 percent with the application of antagonistic Trichoderma fungi onto the rice seed (Khalili et al., 2012). Likewise, in most areas, hot-water seed disinfection or seed dressing with chemicals is advised to reduce seed-borne inoculum (Sunder et al., 2014). Moreover, BLS depends on the type of rice. Although it is not a culture practice, in many cases, the use of planting of resistant or tolerant cultivars is combined with cultural practices. There are some conventional types which have partial resistance to BLS and breeding programs are still working on better lines (Barnwal et al., 2013). The choice of variety by the farmers, which is a culturally and preference-based decision, therefore, contributes to the BLS management. Nevertheless, the moderately resistant ones can still succumb to the conditions, and that is why field practices will be relevant (Surendhar et al., 2022). Planting method and density: The way rice is planted as well as the distance between plants influence the microclimate of the crop and the disease pressure to a great extent. Planting close to the ground and sowing through the air (traditional growing methods) is likely to produce the dense canopy that allows foliar diseases to thrive such as BLS (Sunder et al., 2014). Line transplanting or planting seed in rows with the required spacing, on the contrary, enhances the air movement and sunlight accessibility in the canopy that may shorten the period of wetness on the leaves and limit the sporulation of fungi. Sunder et al. (2014) observe that the occurrence of brown spot can be reduced by adopting appropriate spacing and applying inappropriate levels of seeding to reduce the ability of the pathogen to thrive in a favorable micro environment. Furthermore, direct-seeded upland rice (typical of low-input systems) is usually worse affected by brown spot than flooded rice transplanted, in part due to upland plants being exposed to intermittent drought stress and changes in nutrients that predisposes them to BLS (Bhutia et al., 2025). In India, the example of BLS is reported to be predominantly in dry, direct-seeded rice in such states as Bihar and Chhattisgarh [5]. In the given circumstances, disease is propagated by the lack of standing water and increased stress on higher plants. In cultural sense therefore, the inherent risk of BLS may be indirectly increased by the traditional practice of direct broadcasting on dry soil, but reduced by such practices as promote active early growth (as in nursery transplanting or wet seeding).

Nutrient management and fertilization: Probably the most recorded cultural impact on brown spot is the rice nutritional status of the crop. It is agreed that a balanced fertilization lowers the severity of the brown spots, and nutrient imbalances increase it (Barnwal et al., 2013; Sunder et al., 2014). BLS has been termed to be more common with rice that is planted on poor soil or unfertilized soils - hence the name of it being a poor soil disease. Fields that experienced severe cases of brown spot were usually those that had depleted soils, which lacked enough nitrogen (N) and potassium (Padmanabhan, 1973). Sufficient N fertilization has the potential of enhancing the health of plants and resistance, yet, surprisingly, excessive N may have a comparable effect. In recent research, it is stated that very high rates of nitrogen application are prone to augment the intensity of brown spot [6] [7]. As an example, Kumar et al. (2024) discovered that the N dose and the development of BLS were positively correlated: rice plots with unnaturally high N rate (120 kg/ha) exhibited significantly more leaf spotting, when compared to moderate N rates. The probable reason is that high N causes lush and succulent leaves that are more vulnerable to pathogenic attacks, and can also cause a relative deficient condition of other nutrients (such as potassium) when unbalanced (Sunder et al., 2014). However, on the one hand, vegetation deficient in N may be weaker itself and susceptible to infection, thus, balance is the key. Individually, field experiments showed that split dose (not single dose) application of a recommended N rate in combination with sufficient phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) effectively suppressed brown spot, but single heavy dose of N in the absence of K intensified the disease (Sunder et al., 2014). Specifically, potassium is known to increase the resistance of rice tissues; K-deficient plants become more susceptible to brown spots (Prabhu et al., 2012; Sunder et al., 2014). Similarly, silicon (Si) which is a micronutrient has a protective effect. Si is absorbed into rice easily and strengthens the cell walls and improves host defense. During trials, silicon amendments (e.g. calcium silicate) have made brown spot less severe on rice leaves and grains by more than 50 percent, and have also enhanced grain fill (Prabhu et al., 2012). Therefore, there is a universal recommendation of practices in culture to control brown spot, i.e. balanced fertilization that is not too much N and should not be less than K and Si (Bhutia et al., 2025). A variety of literature discusses brown spot epidemics as one of the symptoms of so-called nutritional disorder in the crop, which can be cured through the effective use of fertilizers (Barnwal et al., 2013). Irrigation and water management: Cultural practice is an interaction between moisture regime and the effect on BLS. The fungus prospers in warm and damp climate; it needs the leaf to be wet 8-24 hours to become severely infected [8][9]. The rainfed rice cultures, particularly in the upland regions with uneven rainfall tend to undergo water stress and then dew or rain that enhances BLS. Drought stress allows plants to get weakened and susceptible to infection (Barnwal et al., 2013). In fact, drought years are often related to epidemics of BLS (Savary et al., 2005). On the other hand, persistent flooding (as in intensive lowland agriculture) may reduce drought stress and hence reduce BLS, although nutrient requirements must be satisfied; BLS of heavily fertilized irrigated crops is still possible under other conditions that are propitious to the pathogen (Kabore et al., 2025). The cultural habit of keeping the flooded paddies or allow the fields to dry may thus influence the level of disease. As an illustration, in certain regions farmers are subjected to regular drainage throughout the season - when it is not well timed, this water management may trigger water stress and tempt the brown spot. Overall, one of the cultural control strategies of brown spot is adequate irrigation to prevent drought (Barnwal et al., 2013). In the meantime, preventing late planting, which causes harvesting of crops in cold and wet climates is another preventive measure; late-harvesting rice during the winter usually matures more brown spot (Sunder et al., 2014). Hence, planting timings (which is a cultural choice) may be changed in such a way that the most sensitive stages (flowering to grain filling) do not overlap with the most favorable conditions. Crop rotation and management of residue: The brown spot pathogen has the ability to survive across seasons on contaminated rice stubble and some weed hosts at and near paddy fields (Kabore et al., 2025). Consecutive rice crop without rotation or leaving rice straw and stubble in the field may cause accumulation of inoculum in the field, which is practiced by traditional farmers. Cultural interventions suggested to be used are the removal or destruction of infected crop residues after the harvest and crop rotation (planting a non-host crop in alternate seasons) to interrupt the disease cycle (Sunder et al., 2014). As an example, the disease-infected rice straw can be burned or composted to destroy the stored spores, and rice can be mixed with another crop (such as legume) and left to rot in a season to significantly decrease the pressure of BLS in the subsequent rice crop (Surendhar et al., 2022). It has been found that in the fields of the farmers in Asia and Africa, the severity of brown spots reduces when these cultural hygiene practices are implemented (Barnwal et al., 2013). Moreover, it is necessary to control the weed in and around the paddy because a number of grass weeds and species of wild rice represent alternative hosts of B. oryzae [10]. The conventional low-input systems occasionally overlook the weed management thus unwillingly letting the pathogen remain on the weeds. Best cultural practice is to ensure that the field remains clean by doing regular weeding or applying herbicides, eliminating the pathogen reservoirs (Surendhar et al., 2022).

All in all, the research, and the experience of farmers demonstrate that the brown leaf spot disease can be significantly alleviated by the use of sound cultural practices. The healthy seed of resistant varieties, optimal density of planting, balanced NPK (with particular focus on Si nutrition), proper irrigation, and absence of weeds and infected debris in the fields are all methods, which help to reduce the incidence of BLS (Bhutia et al., 2025; Sunder et al., 2014; Surendhar et al., 2022). These are the practices that make up the best practices of integrated approaches that should be emulated in BLS all over the world. As an example, Bhutia et al. (2025) highlight the use of cultural, biological, and maximal chemical indicators, i.e., the beginning of resistant seed and equal fertilization, to control brown spot in a sustainable manner [11][12]. In spite of these pieces of advice, in certain traditional farming communities, adoption is not evenly distributed because of socioeconomic reasons as well as limited resources. Therefore, there is a continuous focus on measurement of the benefits of better practices and their effectiveness demonstration, to promote their greater adoption. The current research is based on this body of knowledge, as it experimentally assesses individual changes in cultural practices and quantifies their direct effects on the development and production of brown spot disease and rice yield.
Methodology:

Experimental design: The research was done on field experiments to determine the impact of various cultural practices on the brown leaf spot disease in rice. The experiments were conducted in a research farm (latitude 25degN, tropical monsoon climate) in two seasons of rice planting. The split-plot experimental design was utilized, and three major factors were used, namely: (1) Planting (traditional broadcast seeding and improved line sowing), (2) Nutrient and organic management (conventional fertilization and enhanced fertilization with organic amendment), and (3) Weed management (no weed control and regular weed control). Each treatment combination was done four times in randomized blocks. The type of rice was a medium duration, high yielding cultivar that is moderately susceptible to brown spot (so that disease develops but responds to the practice is improved). Plot size 5 m x 5 m, inter-row spacing, 20 cm, in line-sown plots (ca. 25 hills/m2) as opposed to a similar plant density in broadcast plots through suitably high seeding rate.

Treatment and crop establishment: With line sown plots, the pre-germinated seeds were planted in rows using a mechanical drill, but with broadcast plots they were evenly sown by hand. To provide nutrient management, the traditional fertilization program (a reflection of local farmer management) involved 120kg/ha of nitrogen (in the form of urea) applied in two portions (basal and tillering) and phosphorus and potassium at a rate of 30kg/ha applied basal. A balanced dose of N-P-K was applied in the enhanced fertilization regime: N 80 kg/ha was used in three applications (half of this dose at 15 days after sowing, 25 percent at tillering, 25 percent at panicle initiation), P 30 kg/ha, and K 40 kg/ha were applied at the base stage, and well-decomposed farmyard manure (FYM) was applied at 5 tons/ha spread out before sowing. This superior system was aimed to prevent unreasonable nitrogen and promote soil wellbeing. Silicon supplement was not added specifically, but FYM and soil minerals backgrounded Si. In the case of managing weeds, no weed control was used and the weeds grew naturally throughout the season (the plots replicated a conventional low-input field), and the weeded plots were sprayed out by hand weeding at 20 and at 40 days after germination. Other crop management procedures were standardized in all treatments: all plots were irrigated when necessary to prevent stress of drought and all plots were subjected to standard insect pest management to ensure that variations observed could be attributed to the possible factors of interest and not due to the damage by the pests.

Inoculation and tests of disease: Adequate disease pressure was obtained by enclosing plots with a border of susceptible rice sprayed with a solution of Bipolaris oryzae (10,000 spores/mL) at the latest possible tillering phase. This helped to produce a standard source of inoculum; the further development of the disease would depend on the nature of the spread and conditions. The experiment did not have any fungicides. Incidence and severity of brown leaf spot were observed at the onset of the lesion up to grain filling. The severity of the disease was determined at milk (around 12 weeks after sowing) sampling ten plants per plot, and rating the proportion of the overall leaf area covered by brown spots lesions. This was rated on a standard rating scale (0-9 of the IRRI Rice Disease Evaluation System) transformed into Percent Disease Index (PDI) to be analysed (such that, e.g., many large lesions on most leaves may be taken to represent 50% of the leaf area affected = high severity). Also grain infection was checked at harvest: a random sample of 100 grains per plot was surface-sterilized and incubated to determine the number of grains with the B. oryzae spores on them, which gave a measure of the percentage infection of the seeds (this is complementary to foliar severity, because brown spot may infect grains to give the appearance of pecky rice). At maturity, each plot was harvested and threshed to get grain yield by harvesting 4 m2 in the center (to eliminate edge effects). Yield (tons per hectare at 14 percent moisture) was obtained. Other agronomic measurements were the height of plants, the number of tillers and the fact that there was any significant difference in maturity/ grain filling amongst the treatments. Data analysis: Data collected were analyzed by factorial model of analysis of variance (ANOVA) that was based on split-plot design ( planting method and nutrient regime as main plot factor, weed management as subplot factor). Tukey HSD was done to make mean comparisons with a significance level of p < 0.05. The ANOVA made the arcsine square root transformation of disease severity data (proportions) as a way of stabilizing the variance. The effects of interaction between factors were also investigated to establish whether or not, say, better management of nutrients had more disease-reducing effects with one planting method than with the other. In the same way, weeding was evaluated in terms of its impact on disease in both situations. The dependence between the level of nitrogen and the severity of disease under treatment was also examined using simple linear regression to establish the relationship. The entire statistical work was performed using the SAS 9.4 software. The following section provides the results with the help of a figure that demonstrates the impact of nitrogen fertilization on the severity of brown spots and a table that summarizes the severity of the disease and yield at the various combinations of cultural practices.

Findings: General disease statistics. All the plots developed brown leaf spot during mid teenering stage and aggravated during grain filling. The overall disease pressure was medium to high, which was enough to identify any differences between treatments. There were clear trends that were established in which cultural practices were a major influence on the severity of BLS and subsequent yield. It is interesting to note that plots that were handled with better practices had observably less and smaller lesions on the leaves whereas the practice plots used the traditional way exhibited widespread spots and early browning of leaves. The experimental controls were effective because no other major diseases (e.g. blast or sheath blight) confounded the observations. We report the findings at the individual level and their combinations. Figure 1: Effect of nitrogen fertilizer rate on brown leaf spot severity. Higher N application was associated with a sharp increase in disease severity. Plots receiving an excessive dose of 120 kg N/ha had an average of ~38% leaf area affected by brown spot, compared to ~15–20% in low-N plots (Figure 1). This was a positive relationship between N level and BLS severity (p < 0.01). In practice the rice plants with the highest N had approximately twice the severity of the disease of the lowest N and there was an intermediary severity level with intermediate N rates (60-80 kg/ha). The results verify the previous reports that intensive nitrogen fertilization in the absence of balance may worsen the brown spot infection [6][7]. Significantly, the effect of N interacted with other effects: the effect of high N increasing the disease was most significant in plots where no other improvements were done (i.e. broadcast, unweeded plots) but in the well managed plots the effect of N relative to the increase was smaller (although it was still present). This means that the effect of high N was universal with a tendency to raise the BLS but good agronomy was able to partially compensate the effect.
Impact of mixed cultural practices:

Table 1 shows the summary of the brown spot severity (percent) and grain yield under varying combinations of cultural practices. To make it understandable, three representative treatments are depicted: the case of a Traditional situation, the case of the High-N Conventional situation, and the case of the Improved Integrated

situation. The Traditional (broadcast sowing, no FYM, farmer fertilizer practice, no weeding) situation had an extreme disease severity, with a mean of 28% of the leaf area affected, and a low yield of grain (about 2.1 t/ha). The High-N Conventional (as in traditional but with even greater N rate of 120kg/ha) scenario was poorest with the severity of 38.3 percent and yield at just about 1.9 t/ha. Conversely, the scenario that appeared to be significantly less severe in terms of BLS (only 17.6% severity) and the highest yield (3.13 t/ha) was the Improved Integrated scenario - line sowing at the optimal spacing, FYM amendment, half-way delivery of a moderate dose of N (80 kg/ha), and frequent weed control. The severity of this integrated treatment compared to the high-N conventional treatment was less than half and its yield of grains was about 60 percent more. These differences were found significant using a statistical analysis (p < 0.05 of all pairwise comparisons). The analysis shows that the combination of the cultural practices affects each other in a synergistic way: although each of the individual factors (improved planting approach, balanced N, weeding) had some beneficial effect on the reduction of the disease, the composite of them had the most significant effect.

Additional information was given by other treatment combinations (not completely displayed in Table 1). To illustrate, the severity of the disease when weed control was introduced alone (no other factors altered) was lower by an average of 4-6 percentage points and yield was higher by an average of 0.3 t/ha than the unweeded population, which is important in indicating the contribution of weed hosts towards the disease. In a similar procedure, the use of FYM and division of N (even in the case of broadcast sowing) reduced severity and increased the yield compared to N used singly on soils without FYM. The effect of using the planting method was also observed whereby broadcast vs. line sowing was done under the same inputs: line-sown plots had less brown spot (by approximately 3-5 percent) and yields were slightly higher. This is due to a bigger plant spacing and probably, the seedlings in the line sown plots were stronger. The overall disease incidence was not significantly different in broadcast and line sowing under optimal conditions in other practices, indicating that nutrient and weed control may have a greater effect as compared to planting geometry when disease pressure is high. Poor nutrient/weedy conditions, however, had a significantly greater impact on broadcast plots as compared to line-sown ones (interaction effect was found in ANOVA, p < 0.05). It was noted that the moderately resistant variety, which was used in the Methodology, performed well compared to more vulnerable rice lines which were planted in neighboring demonstration plots. The selected variety (partially resistant to BLS) was of severity approximately 15 percent in the improved practice regime, and a susceptible variety of check reached approximately 30 percent severity in the improved practice regime (data not provided in table). This is in line with other studies by Kumar et al. (2024), which found that a resistant cultivar named Rajshree only showed 12-16% severity despite high severity in the susceptible varieties at 80 kg N/ha. Also, since we used only one cultivar in our research, which gave us consistency, this is an indication that varietal resistance may even increase the rewards of cultural control.

The rate of discoloration and pathogen presence was high in the case of seeds harvested in high-disease plots in terms of grain infection. The rate of B. oryzae infection in grains tested in the high-N no-weeding treatment was 48% (resulting in severe peck and quality loss). In comparison, 10-15% of the grains in the practice plots which had been improved were infected. This variation is vital to the quality of the seed in the following season and marketability of the grain (brown spot-infected grain gets downgraded). Therefore, better cultural practices did not only conserve the health of leaves and yield but also minimized grain spotting and ensured the quality of grain.

On the whole, the findings provide a clear evidence of the strong role of cultural practices on the outcomes of BLS diseases. The worst scenario of brown spot was the case of unbalanced high nitrogen, poor field sanitation (weeds and residues), and high planting- unfortunately, these are the conditions that are still present in resource constrained agriculture. In this case of situation, the severity of the BLS was high and the yields were low. On the other hand the introduction of integrated cultural enhancements resulted in significantly lower disease levels and an increased crop environment not very conducive to Bipolaris oryzae and, therefore, a high productivity. The implications of these findings are discussed in the next section where they are compared with other studies and how the cultural practices regulate brown spot disease mechanisms.
Discussion:

The results of the research confirm that cultural practices play a significant role in determining the process of brown leaf spot disease in rice. The substantial decrease in the severity of BLS in the case of a combined agronomic solution speaks of the fact that this disease, which is commonly seen as a sign of ineffective crop management (Barnwal et al., 2013), can be effectively reduced in the case of the optimization of cultivation methods. In this part, we explain what each of the key practices implies to the results and the current literature. The impact of over-fertilizing with nitrogen to the degree of BLS severity was one of the most vivid effects. Disease had been observed to be much higher in plots with 120 kg N/ha, which is consistent with the report by Kumar et al. (2024) that excess N positively correlates with incidence of brown spots. This could be explained in a number of ways. To begin with, excessive N may result in rich and tender leaves with a higher level of amino acids on their surface, which may increase the infection and colonization of B. oryzae (Sunder et al., 2014). A relative deficiency of other nutrients (such as K) with disease-resistance significance can also be caused by high N, unless the nutrient is also raised in equal proportion, the plant tissues might be more susceptible to invasion by pathogens (Prabhu et al., 2012). There is also an overgrowth of canopy by high N which can create a microclimate of increased humidity under the canopy leading to the germination of spores. This was prevented by our better treatment of moderate N rate with splits, which did not make plants vulnerable, but kept them healthy. It is worth noting that this corresponds to the recommendations on integrated nutrient management that does not encourage the use of unbalanced fertilization. Past researches demand the equal and adequate application of fertilizer to control brown spot [13][11]. The observed dramatic yield penalty at high N level (though N can increase yield, as explained by its potential yield enhancing effect) could have been attributed to disease induced poor grain filling, and possibly, the lodging or physiological stress associated with what can be referred to as luxury consumption of N. It stresses that an increased use of fertilizer is not always good - further than a certain stage it became counterproductive through disease aggravation.

On the other hand, making use of organic manure (FYM) and other potassium benefited the crop. FYM helps improve the soil structure and microbiota and it is also a source of slow-release nutrients. Increased soil health with the help of FYM might increase the vigor of rice and also promote antagonistic microbes in soil which suppresses the B. oryzae inoculum (Khalili et al., 2012). In fact, organic amendments have been linked with decreased foliar disease within certain systems because of resistance induced and enhancement of nutrient availability. The integrated plots that had FYM and divided N in our study looked healthiest and had the lowest brown spot. This observation aligns with the observation of farmers who reported that the severity of brown spot reduces when the rice crop is well fed in a holistic manner and not only with synthetic N (Surendhar et al., 2022).

The other important result was the obvious benefit of adequate field hygiene and an advantage of control of weeds. Disease propagated more freely in areas not weeded - again probably due to weeds providing a green passageway to the pathogen and hampering the flow of air. In comparison, the number of BLS lesions was lower in weeded plots, which is why it is recommended to manage the weed hosts of B. oryzae (Kabore et al., 2025). The fungus may live in weeds like Leersia hexandra and wild rice and they can be found near the rice hills and they produce spores continuously which may settle on the leaves of the rice (Kabore et al., 2025). The elimination of these other hosts ruins this chain. Also, our method of eliminating the old crop debris (by not having stubble cover in the experimental plots) and clean seed meant that initial inoculum was restricted to that which we intentionally added. In actual agriculture, when the farmers practice residue removal or burning - as recommended by Ghose et al. (1960) since the Bengal epidemic - they will probably mitigate primary inoculum loads and by doing so, early disease establishment. This aligns with the concept of integrated disease management that considers crop residue management and crop rotation to decrease the presence of pathogens between in seasons (Sunder et al., 2014; Surendhar et al., 2022).

The planting practice and density yield, although not as dramatic as other factors, still signify the real benefits of the better practice. The spacing of rice plants was done by line sowing at the right spacing, which would have minimized competition and stress among plants. Plants spaced apart were more vigorously growing and their cuticles and silicon uptake might have been more thick and silicon uptake per plant can be concentration-dependent, and a high planting density could dilute soil Si availability per plant. The factors have the potential of increasing resistance to BLS (Rodrigues et al., 2015, in Prabhu et al., 2012). Moreover, improved spacing implies that the leaves will dry quicker following rain or dew and the leaf wetness interval, which is essential to infection, will be reduced [14]. In our experiment, broadcast and line sowing had a buffering effect in that the broadcast plots received an optimal seed rate to prevent objectionable over-crowding. However, broadcast sowing in farmers fields tends to cause clumped germination and greater effective densities as compared to line transplanting. Therefore the advantage of line transplanting may be greater in reality than our measurements. The best overall cultural control, as we find it coupled with experience on the part of the farmers, is the optimum of planting density - excessive crop density encourages heavier brown spot. The time of practices of culture is also worth mentioning. We adhered to the time schedules of planting and ensured that there was sufficient water, which prevented the well-known risk factors such as cold and drought at the end of the season. It is thought that late planting (e.g. seeding after mid-season rains) can subject the crop to colder nights and increased dew during the grain fill, where BLS spores thrive best (Sunder et al., 2014). Other farmers in certain areas like parts of South Asia have customarily planted rice later on in the season due to cultural festivals or availability of labor. The extension message that would come out of such a study would be to plant earlier (where possible) to avoid the high-risk period of brown spot around the end of the season. On the same note, it is vital to ensure that the crop is not stressed due to water scarcity at key points (flowering and grain filling) - B. oryzae takes advantage of physiological stress as observed by increased disease in droughts-prone uplands (Barnwal et al., 2013). The irrigation regime of our experiment ensured the constant availability of moisture that probably contributed to the plants being resistant to infection by avoiding the susceptibility of stress (Hedge et al., 2019). This supports the suggestion that the regular management of water is a cultural disease prevention of brown spot.

One essential aspect that should be taken into consideration is how these cultural controls can be stacked with a genetic resistance to work together synergistically. Although our experiment maintained the same level of variety (except to mention differences in demonstration plots), the scientific sources suggest that even partially resistant varieties will dramatically minimize damage of BLS (Barnwal et al., 2013). Nevertheless, these varieties may not necessarily be available or acceptable to other reasons (yield, grain quality) to farmers. Cultural practices provide an easy way of managing disease without the need of having new seed. However, a combination of both will yield the best results, i.e. a BLS-resistant or tolerant strain and its breeding under optimal agronomy. In practical terms, a farmer which plants a resistant type of rice and practises, as well, such as the ones we looked at (e.g. balanced fertilization, clean seed, crop rotation) has much less to lose economically due to brown spot. This holistic approach is reflected by the latest international evaluations of the BLS management (Kabore et al., 2025) that finds combined practices to be better than exclusive use of fungicides or any tactic [15]. Actually, brown spot fungicides (MCZ or triazoles) can be used to protect leaves [16][17] but are not economically viable to use against farmers with limited resources who grow low-value rice and excessive use may cause environmental and resistance problems. Cultural controls, therefore, give BLS management a more sustainable low costs foundation.

Our findings are in agreement with the findings in different parts of the world. In West Africa, Fomba and Singh (1990) reported losses of up to 8-23% of the yields of traditional mangrove swamp rice due to brown spot which largely occurred in the low-fertilized fields - a situation similar to the situation as in our traditional treatment. As they enhanced activities (with fungicide in that instance), the product output was increased, which suggested that cultural inadequacy significantly contributed to the initial losses. In Nigeria, Aluko (1975) also obtained a yield loss of about 12% due to brown spot and it was more on nutrient-poor farms. Such regional results correspond to the principle evidenced in our study: crops with improved management are less affected by brown spot. We also find that our yield values (around 1.9-3.1 t/ha across treatments) are similar to real-world farm yields when we have different levels of management, small farmers with low levels of inputs tend to actually yield about 2 t/ha or less with visible brown spot, whereas well-supported farms or experiment yield more than 3 t/ha with minimal disease (Savary et al., 2000b). In addition, correlation between heavy BLS and grains discolouring is directly applicable to rice quality - the farmers in Asia had a historic name of heavily spotted grain, pecky rice, which is less expensive or rejected (Ghose et al., 1960). Through the economic quality of grain spotting which has been reduced to 10-50, the better practices have a greater economic payoff than the increased yield.

To the plant pathology view, the processes in which cultural practices affect BLS can be summed up in the disease triangle model (host-pathogen-environment). We were, in effect, able to enhance our practices to render the environment less conducive (with more appropriate spacing, drier canopy and reduced inoculum), and the host more resistant (with improved nutrition and vigor). In the meantime, such practices as crop rotation and seed choice directly decrease the pathogen initial load. In this way we managed to address the three aspects of the disease triangle. It is this combined strategy, which produced such a significant decrease in illness (less than 50% of the severity), which led to the situation. It is possible to conclude that these cultural measures will be essential even in the conditions of climate change (e.g. warmer and more humid temperatures that will raise BLS as Chaudhry and Akhtar (2022) predict in Pakistan). Indeed, with abiotic stresses on crops expected to spread further with the effects of climate change, good agronomic practices would become even more significant to ward off opportunistic diseases such as brown spot against weakened plants. There are certain limitations of our study which can be mentioned. Our experiments were carried out within a controlled research environment; other factors like labor, costs and knowledge may limit the viability of carrying out all the recommended activities on the farmers fields. To use an example, smallholders might not be able to pay the best fertilizer or could be lacking manpower to weed intensively. Thus, a practical implication is that any small step in the right direction can be helpful - e.g. assuming that a farmer can at least apply a little more K fertilizer or treat their seed, the farmer might get less brown spot. The other weakness is that we used two seasons in our study; it would be of great advantage to use multi-year trials to capture different weather effects. Nevertheless, our findings are consistent with long-term observations in most regions, which puts their generalizability with confidence. Further studies may address this cost-benefit feature of these practices in other socioeconomic settings, as well as examine any trade-offs (such as excessively low plant density might lower yield, regardless of disease, therefore the most appropriate spacing must strike a balance between reducing disease and maximizing yield).

Altogether, the discussions above highlight the fact that cultural practices are an effective agent of control of brown leaf spot disease in rice. With the creation of healthier crop conditions, farmers will be able to essentially "grow out of the brown spot situation. The study gives empirical support of extension programs to promote practices like balanced fertilizer application (with sufficient potassium and moderate nitrogen), application of organic soil amendments, correct planting density, comprehensive field sanitation and application of healthy seed. These measures, together with resistant types and facilitated by the adoption of these inoculums by the community at large (as the inoculum can be distributed across the area), can significantly reduce the burden of brown spot on rice production. Cultural controls can be a viable way out of the problem in an age where less and less chemical pesticides are wanted due to the desire to reduce the need to use these agents. The findings that we have got are part of an ever-increasing literature on the subject that will enable rice growers around the world adopt cultural practices that will ensure they control brown leaf spot thus achieving higher yields and grain quality.
Conclusion:

This study illustrates that cultural farming systems have far-reaching impact on brown leaf spot disease of rice development. Based on the field tests, we demonstrated that a combination of better cultural practices - such as use of healthy seed, the use of the best planting practices, balanced and moderate fertilization practices, the use of organic amendments, weeding at the right time, and the management of harvesting residues, can significantly lower the severity of BLS and boost rice yields. Conversely, the conventional methods that were full sown, used too much or too little nitrogen, and did not sanitize their fields were linked to the high occurrence of the disease and the heavy penalty as a result of the disease. Such results confirm the old belief, that brown leaf spot is as much a cultural disease as it is a plant disease. Enhancement of the crop and weakening the environment of the pathogen was a sustainable approach to enhancing the cost-effective defense of BLS as better cultural practices.

At the global level, the implication is evident: the encouragement of the enhanced agronomic practices must become one of the main components of the brown spot disease management programs. Farmers with limited resources, especially, could avail themselves of the practices, because they have fewer inputs to depend on and more knowledge and labor. The measures adopted will include the use of certified disease-free seed, proper crop rotation and disposal of residue and proper use of fertilizer, which will help in breaking the infection cycle of Bipolaris oryzae. Further such cultural controls should be combined with other measures i.e. planting of BLS resistant varieties of rice where possible, and using fungicides as a final measure will offer a solid integrated disease control approach. This is a strategy that would go in line with the objectives of sustainable farming where they are less reliant on chemical control and capitalize on the natural suppression of diseases through good farming practices.

To sum it up, the occurrence of brown leaf spot disease in rice is not a necessity of rice production, but is a mirror of the management of the product. Cultural practice which relieves stress of plants and helps to lessen inoculum are able to keep this disease at minimal levels even in other favorable climatic conditions. The quantitative evidence provided by our study is that brown spot can be effectively checked with the help of improvement of traditional practices using the science. These findings have implications to researchers and extension agents who have to emphasize on imparting cultural control knowledge to agricultural communities globally. To policy makers and agricultural development initiatives, encouraging farmers to adopt such practices (such as training, provision of soil amendments, and facilitation of community-wide residue management) may have a significant positive effect on rice health and yield. The bottom line is that, to safeguard rice, the food bowl of billions, against the evils of diseases such as brown spot, it will be necessary to unite the cultural knowledge with the contemporary agronomic understanding. This piece confirms that in cases of such undertakings, the fruits are healthier rice harvests, less disease outbreaks and more consistent rice yields all over the world.
